li.a: Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung, Beirut Office: Tel al-Zaatar Diaries, The Massacre in Memory
Days of Palestine: The Massacre of Tal al-Zaatar, A Tragedy that Still Haunts the Palestinians
The New Arab (Internet Archive copy): Thousands of victims of Tel al-Zaatar massacre still missing
Palestine Remembered (Internet Archive copy): The Battle of Tel Zaatar, reproducing a declassified US Army study with a former resident's preface

content.p: For seven weeks in the summer of 1976, a Palestinian refugee camp on the eastern edge of Beirut was pounded by artillery, sniped at and cut off from water. On the morning of 12 August the camp fell. What happened to its people that day, and in the weeks before, remains disputed in its numbers and in its blame. Estimates of the dead run from roughly 800 on the final day alone to several thousand over the whole siege. What the sources broadly agree on is the outcome: the camp was destroyed and never rebuilt, and none of them reports any investigation or trial of those responsible.

The camp was Tal al-Za'atar, Arabic for "thyme hill". Its destruction was one episode in the first phase of the Lebanese Civil War, and it is remembered by Palestinians as one of the war's worst atrocities.
content.h2: A camp on the poverty belt
content.p: Palquest, a Palestinian encyclopedia project, records that the League of Red Cross Societies set up the camp in 1949 on private land that had been a British Army base in the Second World War. Its first residents, 1,932 refugees, came from villages in northern Palestine. UNRWA took over services in 1952 and replaced tents with prefabricated barracks, but the camp stayed short of basic infrastructure: open sewers, a main street of about 200 metres, communal toilets.

It sat beside Lebanon's biggest industrial zone, and over time it drew poor Lebanese and Syrian migrants as well as Palestinians. Palquest says residents worked on farms and in factories but, as refugees, were barred under Lebanese law from social security and health insurance. By 1974 the camp had 14,951 Palestinian residents, by Palquest's count. Other sources give larger figures for the population around 1976: the Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung's Beirut office says about 30,000, while a witness-based account in Now Lebanon says about 45,000 before the fighting began.

Control of the camp changed hands after the 1969 Cairo Agreement between the PLO's Yasser Arafat and the Lebanese army. Palquest says Palestinian guerrilla organisations took the place of the Lebanese intelligence post, and Fatah ran workshops there, including one that maintained light weapons. Palquest argues that this military presence, together with the camp's expansion toward the Christian neighbourhoods around it, made it look to those neighbours like a military base rather than a refugee camp.
content.h2: The bus that started a war
content.p: The camp was tied to the event usually taken as the start of the war. On 13 April 1975 a bus carrying passengers back to Tal al-Za'atar was attacked in Ain al-Rummaneh, a neighbourhood held by the Phalangist (Kataeb) militia. Palquest puts the dead at 26, the Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung at about 27 and Now Lebanon at 28, and all three identify the passengers as people from the camp. They differ on where they had been: a military parade in West Beirut (Palquest), a national celebration in Sabra camp (Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung) or a wedding (Now Lebanon).

By the next year the camp was, in the Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung's words, the only Palestinian enclave in East Beirut outside the control of the Christian militias. Palquest describes a plan by the Kataeb and National Liberal parties and their allies to empty the eastern and northern sectors of Beirut of Palestinians and Muslims. It lists the slaughterhouse district of Karantina-Maslakh, the Dbayeh and Jisr al-Basha camps and the Naba'a neighbourhood as targets that fell before Tal al-Za'atar.

A US Army study of the battle, declassified and reproduced on the Palestine Remembered website, dates the first siege to 1 January 1976. It says this was only a blockade of food and medical supplies, because the Christian forces were then hard pressed elsewhere in Beirut. Karantina fell on 18 January. In the study's account, Damour, a Christian town south of Beirut that Muslim and leftist forces overran, supplied a motive of revenge, especially for the National Liberal Party of Camille Chamoun, whose militia launched the attack on Tal al-Za'atar.

The study also says the Christian forces could have left the camp alone for purely military reasons, since the front lines in Beirut had stabilised, and lists other reasons they did not. Palestinians had begun calling the camp "Stalingrad", it says, and the Lebanese army had disintegrated, leaving weapons and men available.

The full assault began on 22 June 1976, by the account of Palquest, the Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung and Mapping MENA. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung says about 8,000 shells fell on the first day. Mapping MENA says the militias launched more than 70 attacks and at times fired shells at a rate of three a minute, and the US Army study gives the same rate. The New Arab puts the total at 55,000 shells over 52 days.

Not every account agrees on who was in the attack. The US Army study counts about 1,800 attackers, made up of roughly 500 Phalangists, 500 from the National Liberal Party, 300 Lebanese army soldiers and about 400 others, and puts about 1,500 Palestinian defenders in the camp at the start. Now Lebanon's own account says the attack was led by the National Liberal Party and that the Kataeb joined only after 27 June. The same article quotes a fighter, Adham, who dates the first day of violent battle to 17 June, not 22 June, and who says the Syrian regime had given the Lebanese right a green light. Days of Palestine, a Palestinian news outlet, says the Syrian army intervened on the side of the Christian militias and shelled the camp with artillery and tanks, and The New Arab says the militias acted with the support of Hafez al-Assad. The US Army study says Syria's army had entered Lebanon on 1 June and that the final offensive had its "tacit approval", with Syrian officers watching the assault from Christian headquarters. Its entry for 11 July lists Christians and Syrians together against Palestinians and Muslims in several sectors, Tel Zaatar among them. The former resident who wrote the preface to the study, by contrast, says Syrian soldiers manned the anti-aircraft guns that defended the camp.

The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung's article, which also summarises a 2022 book by Muhammad Dawood Al-Ali, says the militias sabotaged the water pipes, leaving residents dependent on a single artesian well beside the hospital. Now Lebanon, drawing on witnesses and a 1977 documentary, describes five sources of water for about 25,000 people, one of them a well polluted with corpses. Those who went to fetch water were exposed to snipers. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung says the dead were remembered as "water martyrs", mostly women and children, with 10 to 30 injured a day.

The camp's doctors have left their own accounts. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung names Dr Abdel Aziz AlLabadi and Dr Youssef Iraqi, who it says were among a medical team of just four present throughout. Surgeons operated without electricity, running water or sterile equipment, in rooms under bombardment, according to the same article. Now Lebanon says the Red Cross was refused entry five times before a delegation got in to evacuate the wounded.

The US Army study also describes the siege, from the attackers' side, as slowed by poor militia discipline and by a camp "much better fortified than expected", with tunnels and bunkers. A former resident who wrote a preface to that study on Palestine Remembered disputes this, calling the tunnels a myth. The same writer argues that the defenders stopped starving civilians from surrendering, a claim that comes from one person and is not corroborated in the other pages consulted.

The US Army study dates the start of the final offensive to 10 August. On 11 August, it says, the attackers took the camp's last water source and a key hill, leaving about 300 defenders. It says the camp was captured on the morning of the 12th, with fighting to subdue scattered resistance continuing into the afternoon. In the study's estimate, no more than 4,000 civilians were still in the camp. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung's article, in its account of Al-Ali's work, puts the number at more than 13,000, and describes the last stage as defenders retreating toward the mountains while civilians tried to move toward militia lines.

Palquest says that after 52 days an agreement, mediated by an Arab League envoy, provided for the evacuation of civilians. On the morning set for the evacuation, it says, the militias instead killed about 800 people. Mapping MENA says the militias killed between 1,000 and 1,500 Palestinians, some executed on the spot and others seized while trying to reach West Beirut. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung describes massacres at checkpoints and inside militia-held areas, with medical teams among those targeted, and the deportation of the remaining women and children to West Beirut. Now Lebanon gives 2,000 to 3,000 dead when the camp fell.

Mapping MENA also says many bodies were mutilated and many women raped, and that most victims were buried in unmarked places and never recovered. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung's article, in its account of Al-Ali's book, states that the final attack followed a military plan drawn up by General Michel Aoun and was carried out by right-wing militias and allied Lebanese army units. The former resident's preface to the US Army study also says Aoun was directing the attack. Both are accusations from Palestinian-side writers; the other pages opened here do not mention Aoun.

Palquest says the camp was razed by bulldozers. By its count more than 3,400 people were killed between 22 June and the eve of the evacuation, many still missing. The New Arab reported in 2016 that, according to the Euro-Mediterranean Monitor for Human Rights, only 80 bodies were recovered at first, and that some families got bodies back by paying bribes to the militias. It adds that testimonies place the bodies of victims, children among them, in shallow graves beneath car parks along what used to be the camp's edge.

Mapping MENA says there has been no legal investigation, and that dozens of parents do not know what happened to their children. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung writes that neither the United Nations nor international organisations took steps to hold anyone to account, and links that impunity to the Sabra and Shatila killings of September 1982.

Palquest says Fatah resettled many survivors in Damour, the coastal town emptied of its mostly Christian residents in January 1976. Arafat chose it so the community could stay together. Arafat tasked a Palestinian poet with starting a school there on 31 August 1976, and UNRWA began opening schools there in early 1977. After Israel's invasion in June 1982 the residents dispersed again, to more than twenty places, including the Beddawi and Nahr el-Bared camps in the north; in Beddawi about 250 families formed a district known as Hayy Tal al-Za'atar. In 2011 former residents living in Beirut's Mar Elias camp founded an association that holds an annual commemoration.

The physical place is gone. A Now Lebanon writer who went looking in 2025 found a military esplanade and new buildings, with no stone, plaque or monument. The memory lives in art instead. The Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung lists Mahmoud Darwish's elegy "Ahmad al-Zaatar", published on the day the camp fell; a long poem by the Iraqi poet Muzaffar al-Nawab; and a series of 28 daily canvases that the painter Ismail Shammout made during the siege. It also lists several documentaries, among them a 1977 film made by the Palestinian Film Institute with an Italian partner. Now Lebanon says the original copies were lost after the 1982 Israeli invasion and an Italian-dubbed television version was restored between 2012 and 2014.
